title: White musicians, Bolden, and the move to Chicago
summary: He recounts white players learning jazz, Buddy Bolden, being recruited to Chicago in 1917, King Oliver and Mutt Carey, pay and union, and the 1919 World Series job.

story.theme_name: Chicago: the jazz migration and its clubs
story.community_name: Going north: working the Chicago jazz scene

blocks.x: Mr. Deer, we'd like for you to tell us, for instance, when these white musicians picked up jazz from the Cullen Boys.

Well, they used to come to those places nightly, and they got them so good so they'd say, Well, Deer, you want to take a walk around the block? I said, Yes. Go ahead. I'll rest you up. I'll play clarinet. And so the rest of the instruments, the other boys would rest them up like that. That's the way they started. Mr. Deer, when you were in the Warriors, did you happen to meet Buddy Bolger? I'm sure he must have run into him. Oh, yes. And New Orleans knows about him. There's no question to ask, because he started that jazz off himself. Well, Mr. Deer, let's go to Chicago now. We know you went there. What year did you go, and how did you go about getting up there? I mean, why did you go? Well, I'm going to tell you why. There's two booking agents came from Chicago down there in the red light district where I was playing at Pete Law on Murray and Bienville Street. And they heard my orchestra, and during the intermission, they found out I was to leave at the band, and they had to talk with me. Okay. Now, what year was that, Mr. Deer? You went to Chicago? 1917. 1917. Were there any other jazz bands up there before you? Yeah, there had quite a few. But then that there wasn't a station in Chicago, such as the Dixieland, Manuel Perez, the Creole Band, and I was about the fourth number there, but I hid it in Chicago and stayed there. And in fact, I signed my contract out in New Orleans right there for Chicago. Now, how about, when did King Oliver come? Was that before or after you? That's way after me. My first trumpet player died. And the other one I had, Mud Carey, came to New Orleans, and he said the climate was too cold, so he was marked second trumpet player, so he came to New Orleans and sent King Oliver in his place. He never did come back until King Oliver got to playing with me. Mr. Deer, will you tell us now something about the job situation there in Chicago, where you played and how much and things like that, how often you played? Well, I played at the Deluxe 35th State. That was my first job out of New Orleans. And my salary was $35 a week per man. The leader got $10 extra. Okay. I also played the Dreamland. I played the Royal Garden. What about the unions? What about the unions? You know, sometimes, were they? Oh, yeah. The walking delegates started seeking up the Lawrence, because I was raising too much sand up there. So I had to get in the union up there. Of course, that made a little difference in prices, so our prices up there was $35 a week. Did you consider that a lot more than New Orleans? Oh, yes. New Orleans was that $1750 orchestra. There was no union in the Orleans then? No. Mr. Dewey, I remember seeing a picture of your band in Jazzmen, the famous book on jazz, where you were playing for a World Series in Chicago. Will you tell us something about that? Yes, sir. That's 1919 World Series. That's between, scale between the White Sox and the Cincinnati Black Sox.
